5 
 
4.3.1 
Ignition Mechanisms 
 
Particle Impact — Heat generated when small particles strike a material with sufficient velocity to ignite 
the particle and/or the material.   
 
Particle impact is a very effective ignition mechanism for metals, but less likely to ignite nonmetals 
unless they are very hard.  The characteristic elements necessary for ignition by particle impact are:  
 
• 
particles that can be entrained in the flowing oxygen;  
• 
gas velocities, typically greater than approximately 30 m/s (100 ft/s) (ASTM STP 986); and 
• 
an impact point ranging from 45 degrees to perpendicular to the path of the particle.a,b  
 
Test data show that, in most cases, the particulate must be flammable to produce ignition of the target 
material.  However, some highly reactive materials, such as aluminum and titanium, can be ignited when 
impacted by inert particles.   
 
Example:  Assembly-generated particles traveling at high velocities can cause particle impact ignition by 
striking the body just downstream of the control element of a valve (Figure 3). 
 
 
Figure 3 
Particle Impact Ignition 
                                                     
a  This was concluded from tests conducted using test fixtures that simulated the configuration of the Space Shuttle Type II Main 
Propulsion System oxygen flow control valve.  The Type II test fixtures were fabricated from Inconel 718 with drill points 
downstream the flow control orifice similar to the actual valve and with drill points removed.  The tests were performed at the 
same conditions and using the same particle mixture that ignited and burned the Type II oxygen flow control valve during 
certification testing.  The test conditions were as follows:  600 K oxygen temperature, 4600 psig oxygen pressure, and 10 mg 
of a particle mixture consisting of 26 percent Inconel 718, 29 percent 21-6-9 stainless steel, and 45 percent aluminum 2219 by 
weight.  The Type II Inconel 718 test fixture that contained the drill point ignited and burned on the second test.  The Type II 
Inconel 718 test fixture in which the drill points were removed resulting in an impact angle of 45 o did not ignite or burn when 
subjected to 40 tests.  [The Space Shuttle flow control valve was subsequently redesigned.] 
b  Benz, F.  Summary of Testing on Metals and Alloys in Oxygen at the NASA White Sands Test Facility (WSTF) During the Last 
6 Months.  In RF/DLPippen:kp:09/14/88:5722, WSTF Metals Work Memo, from David Pippen to Director of Materials and 
Processes Laboratory at George C. Marshall Space Flight Center, September 15, 1988.   

--- Page 12 ---
6 
Data:  Particle impact data for metals and nonmetals are located in the latest versions of ASTM 
Manual 36 (2000) and Standard G94 (2005).  In general, copper and nickel-based alloys are resistant to 
ignition by particle impact.  Hard polymers have been ignited in particle impact tests, but limited data 
exist.  
 
Rapid Pressurization — Heat generated when a gas is rapidly compressed from a low pressure to a high 
pressure.  This ignition mechanism is also known as heat of compression or adiabatic compression.   
 
Rapid pressurization ignition is the most effective igniter of nonmetals, but does not ignite bulk metals.  
The characteristic elements for rapid pressurization ignition are: 
 
• 
rapid pressurization, generally occurring in less than 1 s;  
• 
an exposed nonmetal close to the rapidly pressurized dead-end; and  
• 
a pressure ratio that causes the maximum temperature from compression to exceed the situational 
auto-ignition temperature of the nonmetal.  
 
The maximum theoretical temperature from compression can be calculated using the following equation:

title: Oxygen Ignition Mechanisms and Hazards
summary: This section describes multiple ignition mechanisms in oxygen systems including adiabatic compression, flow friction, resonance heating, mechanical impact, and galling/friction. Each mechanism is characterized by specific elements and conditions that can lead to ignition of materials in oxygen environments.
full_text:
--- Page 13 ---
7 
 
Data:  Auto-ignition temperature data for nonmetals are found in the latest versions of ASTM Manual 36 
(2000) and Standard G63 (1999).  Extensive testing in a system consistent with ASTM G74 has 
demonstrated that for initial upstream pressures less than 275 psia and an initial downstream pressure of 
ambient or above, the actual temperature rise (with real heat loss) is too small for ignition to occur.  
 
Flow Friction — Heat generated when oxygen flows across a polymer and produces erosion, friction, 
and/or vibration.  Flow friction is a theoretical ignition mechanism, but current theory suggests that the 
characteristic elements for flow friction ignition include:  
 
• 
nonmetal exposed to flow; and 
• 
flow that produces a vibration in the nonmetal. 
 
Note: Surfaces of nonmetals that are highly fibrous from being chafed, abraded, eroded, or plastically 
deformed may render flow friction heating affects more severe.   
 
Examples: A leak past a polymer seal may cause flow friction ignition.  This could occur when throttling 
flow through an oxygen cylinder valve with a nonmetal seat that has been damaged due to extensive 
cycling. 
 
Note:  Although this ignition mechanism is poorly understood, it has caused a significant number of real-
life fires. 
 
Resonance — Acoustic oscillations within resonant cavities that cause rapid temperature rise.  The 
characteristic elements for resonance ignition include: 
 
• 
a favorable system geometry, which includes a throttling device (e.g., nozzle, orifice, regulator, or 
valve) directing a sonic gas jet into a cavity or closed-end tube (Figure 5);  
• 
acoustic resonance (often audible) and  
• 
flammable materials in the area of the resonance.  
 
The distance between the throttling device and the closed end affects the frequency of acoustic 
oscillations in the cavity due to the interference of incident and reflecting sound waves.  The distance also 
affects the temperature produced in the cavity.  Higher harmonic frequencies have been shown to produce 
higher system temperatures.  The resonant frequency has been shown to be a function of pipe diameter 
and pressure ratio (f (D, P/Pa)).  
 
Flammable materials residing at or near the closed end of the cavity can self-ignite due to the high gas 
temperatures produced by resonance heating.  Alternatively particulate or debris can vibrate, causing 
collisions that generate sufficient heat to self-ignite.   
 
Examples:  A capped tee fitting downstream of a valve or orifice, similar to Figure 5, can lead to 
resonance ignition.  Resonance is also used as an igniter for solid or liquid rocket fuel: gaseous oxygen 
flows through a sonic nozzle and directly into a resonance cavity, heating the gas and solid or liquid fuel.  
When the gas reaches the auto-ignition temperature of the fuel, ignition occurs and a flame jet is emitted 
from the chamber. 
 
Mechanical Impact — Heat generated due to single or repeated impacts on a material with sufficient 
energy to ignite it.  Most metals cannot be ignited by mechanical impact; however, nonmetals are 
susceptible to ignition by mechanical impact.  The characteristic elements for mechanical impact ignition 
are:  
 

--- Page 14 ---
8 
• 
a single, large impact or repeated impacts; and  
• 
a nonmetal or reactive metal at the point of impact.  
 
Some components, such as check valves, regulators and relief valves, may become unstable and “chatter” 
during use.  Chattering can result in multiple impacts in rapid succession on polymer poppets or seats 
within these components, creating a mechanical impact ignition hazard. The presence of liquid oxygen 
(instead of gaseous oxygen) may cause some porous materials to become dramatically more sensitive to 
mechanical impact. 
 
Example: A wrench dropping onto a porous hydrocarbon (e.g., asphalt) soaked with liquid oxygen could 
cause mechanical impact ignition (Figure 6).

Data: Most metals are not susceptible to ignition by mechanical impact.  However, data has shown that 
aluminum, magnesium, titanium, and lithium-based alloys, as well as some lead-containing solders, can 
be ignited by mechanical impact.  Mechanical impact ignition data for nonmetals are found in the latest 
versions of ASTM Manual 36 (2000) and Standard G63 (1999). 
 
Galling and Friction — Heat generated by the rubbing of two or more parts together.  The characteristic 
elements for frictional ignition are: 
 
• 
two or more rubbing surfaces, generally metal-to-metal;  
• 
rapid relative motion; and 
• 
high loads pressing the rubbing parts together. 
 
Data from ASTM Manual 36 (2000) indicate that metals, not polymers, are most susceptible to ignition 
by friction in the frictional heating tests currently available.  Research indicates that polymers may also be 
susceptible to ignition in certain conditions.  Some components, such as check valves, regulators, and 
relief valves, may become unstable and “chatter” during use.  Chattering can result in rapid oscillation of 
the moving parts within these components, creating a frictional ignition hazard. 
 
Example:  Damaged or worn soft goods resulting in metal-to-metal rubbing between the piston and the 
cylinder of a reciprocating compressor (Figure 7) could lead to frictional ignition.  
 
Data:  Frictional heating data for various pairings of materials is located in the latest versions of 
ASTM Manual 36 (2000) and Standard G94 (2005).

title: Ignition Mechanisms, Kindling Chain Analysis, and Reaction Effect Assessment
summary: This section defines seven primary ignition mechanisms in oxygen systems (impact/friction, rapid pressurization, adiabatic compression, fresh metal exposure, static discharge, electrical arc, and chemical reaction), establishes methodology for evaluating kindling chain propagation through component materials, and provides a four-level reaction effect rating system (A-D) based on personnel safety impact, system objectives, and functional capability consequences.
full_text:
--- Page 16 ---
10 
Fresh Metal Exposure — the heat of oxidation released when unoxidized metal is exposed to an oxidizing 
atmosphere.   
 
This ignition mechanism usually acts in conjunction with other ignition mechanisms, such as frictional 
heating or particle impact, which damage metal surfaces.  This ignition mechanism may also be present 
with a fracture or tensile failure of an oxygen-wetted pressure vessel.  The characteristic elements for 
fresh metal exposure ignition are:  
 
• 
metal that oxidizes quickly and has a high heat of formation for its oxides, such as aluminum and 
titanium alloys;  
• 
destruction or rapid removal of oxide layer; and  
• 
configuration that minimizes heat loss.   
 
Static Discharge — Discharge of accumulated static charge with enough energy to ignite the material 
receiving the charge.  The characteristic elements for static discharge are:  
 
• 
static charge buildup from flow or rubbing accumulated on an electrically isolated surface; and 
• 
discharge point between materials, generally with differing electrical potentials.   
 
Generally, two charged surfaces are not as likely to arc unless one material is conductive.  Static 
discharge ignition is most likely to occur in dry gas environments. 
 
Examples:  Static charge accumulation due to dry oxygen flow through polymer hoses can lead to static 
discharge.  Bed sheets in hyperbaric chambers can be ignited by static discharge. 
 
Electrical Arc — Sufficient electrical current arcing from a power source with enough energy to ignite the 
material receiving the arc.  The characteristic elements necessary for ignition by electrical arc are:  
 
• 
an electrical power source; 
• 
an arc with sufficient energy to melt or vaporize materials; and 
• 
flammable material exposed to heating from the arc. 
 
Example:  A defective pressure switch could cause ignition when it arcs to a flammable material.  An 
insulated electrical heater element undergoing a short circuit could produce ignition by arcing through its 
sheath to a combustible material. 
 
Chemical Reaction — A reaction of a combination of chemicals that could release sufficient heat energy 
to ignite the surrounding materials.   
 
The characteristic elements for chemical reaction ignition depend on the reactants involved.  For example, 
some mixtures may be self-igniting while others need an external heat source.  In oxygen-hydrogen 
mixtures, the ignition energy is so low that it is assumed that energies released from mixing will ignite the 
mixture.  
 
Examples:  Oxygen reacting with the palladium getter in a vacuum-jacketed vessel produces ignition.  
Hydrogen leaking into the oxygen section of an oxygen-hydrogen fuel cell system can produce a chemical 
reaction ignition.  A heat-producing chemical reaction can occur when aluminum is sheared in the 
presence of polychlorotrifluoroethylene (PCTFE).  
 
Thermal Runaway — some materials, notably certain accumulations of fines, porous materials, or liquids, 
may undergo self-sustained reactions that generate heat.  

--- Page 17 ---
11 
 
If the rate of heating compared to the rate of dissipation is unfavorable, the material will increase in 
temperature.  In some cases, a thermal runaway may be attained and some time later the material may 
spontaneously ignite.  Ignition and fire may occur after short time periods (seconds or minutes) or over 
long time periods (hours, days, or months).  In the most extreme cases, the thermal runaway temperature 
may be near or below normal room temperature.  The characteristic elements for thermal runaway 
ignition include:  
 
• 
a material with a high surface-area-to-volume ratio (e.g., dusts, particles, foams, chars, etc.) that 
reacts exothermically (e.g., oxidation or decomposition) at temperatures significantly below its 
ignition temperature and  
• 
an environment that does not adequately dissipate heat (e.g., an insulated or large volume vessel 
or an accumulation of fines). 
 
Examples:  Ignition could occur due to an accumulation of small particulate generated by rubbing and 
abrasion in an oxygen compressor that has been proof-tested with nitrogen gas and is then exposed to 
oxygen.  Contaminated adsorbent or absorbent materials, such as molecular sieves (zeolites), alumina, 
and activated carbon, may become highly reactive in oxygen-enriched atmospheres. 
 
Other—Potential ignition sources to consider should initially include any external heat sources.  Many of 
the potential sources of heat are self-explanatory and include: lightning, explosive charges, personnel 
smoking and open flames, fragments from bursting vessels, welding, and exhaust from combustion 
engines. 
 
4.4 
Determine the Kindling Chain 
 
The ability of a fire to propagate and burn through a component, i.e., the kindling chain, shall be 
evaluated.  Kindling chain begins when a material is ignited, and the material’s heat of combustion is 
sufficient to heat and ignite the surrounding materials leading to a burn-through of the component.  A 
burn-through is considered unlikely when the materials are nonflammable or an unfavorable ignition 
configuration is present.  A burn-through is considered likely when most materials (including the body) 
are flammable and a favorable ignition configuration is present.   
 
An example of a component with a possible kindling chain could be a manual valve with a polysulfone 
seat and a stainless steel stem and body.  In this configuration and at high pressures, the seat, stem and 
body are flammable.  If the polysulfone seat were ignited (e.g., by flow friction or rapid pressurization) 
enough energy could be released to ignite and burn the stem, which could then ignite the body and result 
in a burn-through of the manual valve.  The analyst should assess the kindling chain based on the 
presence of ignition mechanisms and the ability of the materials of construction to contain a fire.  If a 
component could be breached, a kindling chain is present. 
 
4.5 
Analyze the Reaction Effect 
 
The reaction effect shall be determined.  The effects of a fire on personnel, mission, and system 
objectives are assessed by determining the reaction effect.  This value is primarily assigned based on the 
presence of a kindling chain and the potential consequences of a fire.  The potential consequences of a 
fire are based on the extent of fire propagation in the materials that surround the component.  A guide for 
rating the reaction effect for a system can be found in Table 3.  The example column in Table 3 
demonstrates how reaction effect ratings can be applied.

title: Oxygen Compatibility Assessment Process and Hazard Control
summary: This section describes the systematic process for conducting oxygen compatibility assessments, including evaluation of history of use, documentation of results, and implementation of hazard control measures through a structured table format. The hazard control table prioritizes components by reaction effect rating and tracks ignition mechanism mitigation recommendations.
full_text:
--- Page 19 ---
13 
 
 
For example, a manually operated regulator constructed of nonflammable materials with a viable ignition 
mechanism and the absence of a kindling chain would be assigned “negligible.”  The same regulator with 
a kindling chain would be given a higher reaction effect rating of “catastrophic” because personnel could 
be injured or killed if the regulator failed.  Because it is difficult to conceive all possible fire scenarios 
resulting in injury, reaction effect ratings are often applied conservatively, which means the worst-case 
scenario drives the reaction effect assessment.   
 
4.6 
Identify the History of Use 
 
The relevant history of use shall be evaluated.  The history of use is determined by whether the 
component has experienced routine operation/cycling in similar or more severe conditions over an 
extended period of time.  History of use is assigned a rating of either (+) successful, (-) negative, or (?) 
unknown.  For example, if a valve has been used in similar or more severe conditions over a period of 
time then the component may be given a (+) to indicate a successful history of use. 
 
4.7 
Report the Results of the Analysis 
 
The results of the compatibility assessment shall be documented.  An oxygen compatibility 
assessment report can facilitate the communication and dissemination of the results to interested parties 
and record the findings for future reference.  The oxygen compatibility assessment report may also 
recommend changes to design, materials, and procedures in order to mitigate the fire hazards identified.   
 
Figures 8 and 9 provide an example of an oxygen compatibility assessment showing the complete 
analysis of a single component.  Complete and thorough information is extremely beneficial in 
communicating the findings of the assessment.  Whenever possible, references to the data used in 
determining the various ratings should be included.  Pictures, drawings, and schematics of the component 
should also be referenced and included in the final report. 
 
A system-level oxygen compatibility assessment should contain the compatibility assessment charts and 
drawings for each component in the system.  A system description and flow schematic should also be 
included in the final report.  A concise listing of the most severe hazards and suggested mitigations for 
those same hazards shall be included in the oxygen compatibility assessment report.   
 
Once prepared, the report should be reviewed by other analysts to obtain consensus.  Comments and 
feedback should be considered when finalizing the report.  After a final review, the report should be 
archived and transmitted to the customer.  
 
4.8 
Hazard Control Table 
 
Each component should be listed in a table in order of decreasing reaction effect rating similar to Table 4.  
The table records the component, schematic reference, ignition hazard, initial ignition mechanism rating, 
reaction effect, recommendations to control that ignition mechanism, and the resulting ignition 
mechanism rating after the recommendation has been implemented.  Such a table is needed for displaying 
the hazards determined by the oxygen compatibility assessment as well as the current status of the 
recommendations.

13.  ABSTRACT (Maximum 200 words)
 
Understanding and preventing fire hazards is necessary when designing, maintaining, and operating oxygen systems.  Ignition risks 
can be minimized by controlling heat sources and using materials that will not ignite or will not support burning in the end-use 
environment.  Because certain materials are more susceptible to ignition in oxygen-enriched environments, a compatibility assessment 
should be performed before the component is introduced into an oxygen system. This document provides an overview of oxygen fire 
hazards and procedures that are consistent with the latest versions of American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) Standards 
G63 (1999) and G94 (2005) to address fire hazards associated with oxygen systems.  This document supersedes the previous edition, 
NASA Technical Memorandum 104823, Guide for Oxygen Hazards Analyses on Components and Systems (1996). The step-by-step 
oxygen compatibility assessment method described herein (see Section 4) enables oxygen-system designers, system engineers, and 
facility managers to determine areas of concern with respect to oxygen compatibility and, ultimately, prevent damage to a system or 
injury to personnel.

title: NASA Oxygen System Safety Standard - Preface
summary: This document establishes uniform NASA guidelines for oxygen system design, materials selection, operation, storage, and transportation. The standard applies to NASA Headquarters and all Field Installations with minimum requirements, while individual programs may develop additional requirements as needed. The document uses mandatory language ('shalls' and 'wills') to denote requirements referenced in other existing aerospace industry documents.

title: Chapter 1: Basic Oxygen Safety Guidelines - Sections 100-104
summary: This document establishes foundational guidelines for safely storing, handling, and using gaseous and liquid oxygen. It emphasizes that while oxygen is chemically stable and non-flammable itself, it is a strong oxidizer that vigorously supports combustion, with reactivity increasing with pressure, temperature, and concentration. The standard requires proper personnel training, material compatibility knowledge, and system design practices to eliminate ignition hazards.

key_points: Oxygen is a strong oxidizer that vigorously supports combustion despite being chemically stable and non-flammable
Reactivity of oxygen increases with increasing pressure, temperature, and concentration
Most metals and nonmetals are flammable in high-pressure oxygen environments
Personnel handling oxygen must be trained in physical/chemical properties, material compatibility, cleanliness requirements, and system limitations
Material use requires approval through center safety policy including Materials and Processes (M&P) approval
Highly reactive materials must be avoided; less reactive materials may be used if protected from ignition sources
Ignition sources include friction, heat of compression, static discharge, particle impact, and fresh metal surface exposure

Oxygen is a strong oxidizer that vigorously supports combustion despite being chemically stable and non-flammable Reactivity of oxygen increases with increasing pressure, temperature, and concentration Most metals and nonmetals are flammable in high-pressure oxygen environments Personnel handling oxygen must be trained in physical/chemical properties, material compatibility, cleanliness requirements, and system limitations Material use requires approval through center safety policy including Materials and Processes (M&P) approval Highly reactive materials must be avoided; less reactive materials may be used if protected from ignition sources Ignition sources include friction, heat of compression, static discharge, particle impact, and fresh metal surface exposure

summary: This section provides guidelines for selecting nonmetallic materials (polymers, elastomers, plastics, thermosets, composites, and lubricants) for oxygen service. Key ignition sources include adiabatic compression heating during pressurization, mechanical impact, and contamination with incompatible oils and greases.

title: Section 303 - Metallic Materials for Oxygen Service
summary: Comprehensive guidance on selection criteria and properties of metallic materials for oxygen systems, with emphasis on ignition resistance, oxide coating formation, and specific alloy families including nickel-iron and nickel-copper alloys. Discussion covers how protective oxide layers, thermal properties, and composition affect material suitability for high-pressure oxygen applications.

material_records.compatibility_notes: Marginally less ignitable than stainless steels. Good structural material with exceptional low-temperature toughness. Resists ignition by particle impact better than most stainless steels but similar to stainless steel 440C. Ignites at Pv products similar to stainless steels in frictional heating tests. Used extensively in high-pressure oxygen systems.

Exceptional resistance to ignition by frictional heating. Does not support self-sustained combustion (0.32-cm diameter rod burning upward) at pressures as high as 69 MPa (10000 psia). Superior performance compared to standard Inconel alloys.

Least ignitable alloy commonly used as structural material. Has not ignited in particle impact tests (surface melting and burning may occur). Does not burn upward in upward flammability tests even at oxygen pressures as high as 69 MPa (10000 psia). Ignites in frictional heating tests only at higher loads than stainless steels, and fire does not propagate. Unusually high friction coefficient values.

Least ignitable alloy commonly used as structural material. Has not ignited in particle impact tests (surface melting and burning may occur). Does not burn upward in upward flammability tests even at oxygen pressures as high as 69 MPa (10000 psia). Ignites in frictional heating tests only at higher loads than stainless steels, and fire does not propagate. High friction coefficient values.

Forms protective passivating oxide film as stoichiometric compound. Cannot be used for temperatures above 800°C (1470°F) because it volatilizes. Good protection against oxidation but temperature limited.
Stoichiometric compound providing good oxidation protection. Poor thermal shock resistance, not suitable for thermal cycling applications. Limited performance in dynamic temperature environments.

Good choice for protective oxide coating but requires high temperatures above 1000°C (1830°F) for easy formation. Very limited ductility, cannot withstand thermal cycling and thermal shock, and tends to spall. Adding reactive elements in small amounts to alumina-forming alloys can avoid spalling up to high temperatures.
Non-protective coating material in metals. Not stoichiometric line compound, resulting in high diffusion through vacancies and interstitials. Does not provide adequate oxygen barrier protection.

title: Section 303f - Restricted Materials in Oxygen Systems
summary: NASA safety standards prohibiting or severely restricting use of titanium, cadmium, beryllium, magnesium, and mercury in oxygen systems due to high flammability, toxicity, and impact sensitivity. Titanium is explicitly forbidden with LOX at any pressure and with GOX above 30 psia due to extremely low ignition thresholds and ability to sustain combustion at pressures as low as 1 psia.

summary: NASA safety standards for oxygen systems require integrated safety assessment throughout design review phases (PDR, FMEA, CDR, SSA/SR) and component/system testing. Design reviews must evaluate all aspects down to individual part level, address single-point and single-barrier failures, and review all ignition modes. Component and system testing should be conducted with clean oxygen after hazards analysis, including prototype development testing and qualification testing with worst-case operating conditions.

Designers must thoroughly understand reactivity of selected materials in oxygen-enriched environments
Materials should be evaluated for ignitability and flammability over their intended operating range
Flammability tends to increase with increasing temperature and pressure
Multiple ignition mechanisms must be considered: mechanical impact, pneumatic impact, particle impact, promoted combustion, frictional heating, electrical arcing, and single-barrier failures
Surface preparations (coatings, platings, hard-facings) should be avoided when possible; when necessary, cleaning procedure effects must be evaluated
Specific strength (strength-to-density ratio) should be leveraged to use oxygen-compatible materials like Monel K-500 instead of less compatible lightweight metals
Fluorinated lubricants approved for oxygen usage should be used
Design must account for thermal expansion and contraction differences between polymers and metals to prevent seal leaks
Filters should isolate system particulate at module inlets/outlets, disconnect points, and upstream of valve seats
Design should incorporate fire containment methods such as fire break, fire blow-out, or remote operation
Material properties (strength, ductility, hardness) must be evaluated across all operating conditions

key_points: Kel-F and other nonmetallic materials subject to feathering should only be used with caution for seals and seats in rotating configurations

Thin walls between cavities and outer surfaces can rupture under pressure, releasing energy that raises temperature and may ignite exposed bare metal

material_records.compatibility_notes: Subject to feathering - thin, feather-like projections of material are extruded from the seat. Feathered material is more ignitable than the seat itself. Should only be used with caution for seals and seats in rotating configurations.

Successful in static environments but usually poor choices in dynamic environments. Increased wear or accelerated extrusion on unusual seat shapes. Should only be considered in designs where exposure to oxygen is minimized, such as line exposure. Cold flow is a concern - soft goods with little resiliency permanently deform resulting in sealing loss.
Used for seals where elastomers must be used and cannot be limited to line exposure. Configuration exposes the most compatible materials preferentially to oxygen.
Used as seats in valves and regulators. Noncompliance of material requires small contact area with hard mating surface (metal or sapphire) to achieve seal.

Not recommended for oxygen systems. May be found in existing systems. Excessive cross-linking in oxygen environments may occur, leading to embrittlement and degradation. Careful examination during maintenance procedures is recommended.

Often used for oxygen seals and can provide very reliable seal. At extremely high temperatures, copper oxide that forms on exposed surfaces can dislodge from substrate, becoming a source of particulate contamination.
Alternative to rigid plastics for use as seats in valves and regulators if precautions to eliminate galling have been taken.

Required for hot oxygen at high temperatures and pressures. Both poppet and bore surfaces may be hardened by nitriding or similar process to minimize material loss by fretting or galling and resist ignition by frictional heating.

key_points: Material requirements for LOX are similar to GOX with additional consideration for material embrittlement at cryogenic temperatures
Vaporization of LOX around heat sources such as ball bearings increases ignition risks and requires pressure compensation
Thermal conditioning of cryogenic systems is mandatory with bypass flowpath and pressure relief valves
LOX pump startup must be carefully analyzed to avoid cavitation-induced pressure increases and frictional heating ignition
Condensation on external and internal surfaces must be avoided to prevent ice formation and hazardous conditions
Long-term LOX storage and cyclic operations may concentrate low-volatile impurities requiring periodic vessel analysis
Material cracking and fractures from low-temperature embrittlement can cause premature component failures
Oxygen equipment should not be operated over asphalt pavement due to shock sensitivity and ignition potential
Liquid lockup, fluid expansion, cavitation, and geysering must be prevented through proper design and pressure relief protection
Electrical wiring inside LOX tanks must be encased in hermetically sealed conduits or inerted with helium/nitrogen gas
LOX storage vessels must include inner tank with outer insulation jacket and comply with ASME and CGA standards

Key requirements include material compatibility specifications, velocity restrictions, thermal management for cryogenic service, and protection against overpressure and mechanical hazards. searchable_text: Pressure-Relief Devices and Cylinder Safety Requirements for Oxygen Systems This section establishes requirements for pressure-relief devices, safety valves, and cylinder connections in gaseous oxygen (GOX) systems. It covers relief valve installation, testing, material selection, discharge piping design, and acceptable flexible connectors for cylinders, with emphasis on ignition hazard mitigation in high-pressure oxygen environments. Relief valves and rupture disks must be installed on tanks, lines, and component systems to prevent overpressurization Relief devices and downstream vent lines must be constructed from ignition-resistant materials due to self-activating ignition hazards in oxygen systems Relief valves must be functionally tested in both static and dynamic states to verify design requirements Discharge lines for safety and vent valves should be located outdoors or piped outdoors to discharge in safe areas Stainless steel tubing is the preferred flexible connector for cylinder hookups; Teflon-lined hoses may be used with careful pneumatic impact ignition controls Relief valve riser pipes on high pressure oxygen systems must be analyzed for resonant tuning Stainless Steel Tubing CompatibilityClass.A O2 Flexible Metal Tube/Bellows Sections CompatibilityClass.A O2 Teflon-lined Flexible Hoses CompatibilityClass.B O2 Ignition-Resistant Materials CompatibilityClass.A O2

title: Electrical Wiring and Equipment in Oxygen-Enriched Atmospheres
summary: Guidelines for electrical equipment design and installation in oxygen-enriched environments require compliance with maximum proposed pressure and oxygen concentration conditions. Electrical wiring and equipment must be designed to withstand the operational parameters of the oxygen system, with supplementary guidance available in NFPA 53 (1994).

title: Chapter 5: Cleaning - General Requirements and Safety
summary: This section establishes critical cleaning procedures for oxygen systems and components to prevent functional anomalies and ignition hazards. It addresses the phaseout of ozone-depleting solvents (CFCs) and introduces alternative cleaning methods while emphasizing the importance of disassembly cleaning, operator training, and proper ventilation during cleaning operations.

All components requiring reassembly must be performed in clean rooms or flow benches with personnel in clean room garments O-ring seals must not be forced into bores without adequate chamfers to prevent feathering and particle generation Threaded connections in oxygen systems generate contaminants during engagement and tightening and require careful assembly Press-fit assemblies should be performed with bore opening pointing downward to prevent contaminant entry into flow paths Welded, soldered, and brazed joints should be full-penetration with ground smooth surfaces to prevent slag, porosity, and cracks Burr and sharp edge removal is critical, especially in small-diameter internal passageways and cross drills Hydrocarbon-based lubricants are strictly prohibited in high-pressure and LOX systems due to ignition risk Highly fluorinated lubricants are preferred for oxygen compatibility but require compatibility testing for shock sensitivity O-rings  O2 Hydrocarbon-based lubricants CompatibilityClass.X O2 Highly fluorinated lubricants CompatibilityClass.A O2 Hardened steel  O2 Nonmetallic inserts (screw-locking devices)  O2

summary: This section addresses safety requirements for bulk gaseous oxygen (GOX) and liquid oxygen (LOX) storage systems, including proper location, isolation from combustible materials, component design standards, and hazard analysis methodologies. Key focus areas include preventing adiabatic compression ignition in valves and regulators, controlling oxygen-enriched atmospheres, and maintaining physical separation from flammable materials.

Combined storage-run tanks for LOX have more demanding design and construction requirements than storage-only vessels due to increased pressure and flow requirements
Fire-extinguishing systems for oxygen-enriched atmospheres require specialized design; standard systems designed for normal atmosphere may be ineffective
Automatic fire detection and suppression systems with rapid discharge capability (deluge type) are recommended for oxygen-enriched environments
Early detection of fires in smoldering stages using air-sampling particle detection systems is preferred before visible flames
Water is the most effective extinguishing agent when sufficiently applied; carbon dioxide has limited effectiveness in oxygen-enriched atmospheres

Evacuation plans and personnel training are essential for protection from fire exposure, toxic gas exposure, and extinguishing agent exposure

Emphasizes compliance with ASME codes for vessel design, the critical importance of trained personnel and automatic fire detection/suppression systems, and the limitations of standard fire-extinguishing agents in oxygen-enriched atmospheres requiring specialized design approaches. title: Barricades and Quantity-Distance Guidelines for Bulk Liquid Oxygen Storage
summary: This section establishes safety requirements for barricades surrounding liquid oxygen (LOX) storage and use facilities to protect personnel, equipment, and adjacent areas from blast waves and fragments. Quantity-distance criteria are provided for separating LOX storage systems from inhabited buildings and public traffic routes, with compatibility groups and explosive equivalent factors for fuel-oxidizer combinations.

key_points: Oxygen detection systems must be carefully maintained, periodically recalibrated, and integrated with fire detection systems to initiate corrective actions quickly
Critical detector locations include valve complexes, LOX containers, exposed LOX lines, and vacuum-jacketed equipment discharge points
Uncontaminated LOX should be disposed of through contained vaporization systems (direct-contact steam or heat sink vaporizers), never ground dumped
Contaminated LOX presents long-lived impact-sensitive hazards and requires area isolation, personnel evacuation, and thorough GN2 inerting before cleanup
Gaseous oxygen venting systems must be unobstructed, properly sized to prevent backpressure, located at highest points with vertical exhaust, and positioned away from personnel areas
Vent systems must account for both oxygen enrichment and oxygen depletion hazards with adequate natural dilution distance
Vent-stack design must include rain/snow/ice protection, screens for pest prevention, and low-point drip legs to prevent freezing blockage

material_records.compatibility_notes: Used in heat sink vaporizers for LOX disposal. Must be clean to avoid contamination issues.
Required for disposal and vent systems. Must be maintained at required cleanliness level.

summary: Safety separation distances required between bulk gaseous oxygen storage facilities and various categories of flammable gases stored aboveground. title: Chapter 8: Transportation of Gaseous and Liquid Oxygen
summary: NASA transportation standards for GOX and LOX on public and site-controlled thoroughfares must comply with federal and state regulations (49 CFR and 29 CFR). Gaseous oxygen is classified as UN 1072 (nonflammable gas, oxidizer) and liquid oxygen as UN 1073 (cryogenic liquid, nonflammable gas, oxidizer). Personnel handling hazardous materials require HAZMAT training and emergency response procedures must be established.

LOX is a cryogenic liquid that boils at -297.35°F and is completely miscible with liquid nitrogen and fluorine, while GOX is a colorless gas that vigorously supports combustion at standard conditions.

title: Metal Test Data - Ignition and Flammability Testing Methods
summary: NASA employs three primary test methods for evaluating metallic materials' ignition and flammability in oxygen systems: promoted combustion test (upward flammability), frictional heating test, and particle impact test. The document describes test apparatus specifications, mechanical impact testing procedures, autoignition temperature methods, friction ignition testing, and particle impact testing methodologies for assessing relative material rankings and ignitability characteristics.

key_points: Promoted combustion test system uses 740 cm³ stainless steel chamber pressurizable to 68.9 MPa (10,000 psia) with copper liner and aluminum promoter for ignition testing
Three primary NASA test methods: promoted combustion test, frictional heating test, and particle impact test provide relative material rankings but rarely absolute ignitability information
Upward flammability test (NHB 8060.1C 1991) is primary method for basic ranking of metallic materials' flammability in oxygen service
Frictional heating ignitability is lower in LOX than in GOX due to low initial temperatures, but propagation is more extensive due to large oxygen quantity in condensed phase
Particle impact testing uses supersonic aluminum particles at inlet pressure of 27.5 MPa (4000 psig) with target pressure varying 3.6-4.0 MPa (520-580 psia) and particle velocity 370-430 m/s
Metallic powders are more likely to cause particle impact ignition than large single particles; relative material ranking assumed similar between large particles and powders

test_procedures.test_purpose: Evaluate potential ignition of metals from gaseous pneumatic impact
test_procedures.acceptance_criteria: Metals shown not to ignite from gaseous pneumatic impact

test_procedures.test_purpose: Evaluate ignitability of metallic materials by frictional heating; applicable when frictional heating is a concern
test_procedures.acceptance_criteria: Relative ranking based on Pv product (energy absorbed per unit area per unit time); materials with low Pv products more easily ignited

test_procedures.test_name: Particle Impact Test (Large Single Supersonic Particles)
test_procedures.test_purpose: Evaluate relative ranking of metallic materials' resistance to ignition by impact of supersonic aluminum particles; assess ignitability when particle impact can occur
test_procedures.acceptance_criteria: Relative material ranking based on ignition response (ignition, partial burn, or no ignition) as function of target temperature; target pressure 3.6-4.0 MPa (520-580 psia); particle velocity 370-430 m/s (1200-1400 ft/s)

test_procedures.test_purpose: Evaluate ignition potential of fine metallic particles impacting static targets at low flow velocities
test_procedures.acceptance_criteria: Fine iron particles ignited at velocities as low as 35 m/s (115 ft/s); burning particles ignite targets above 40 m/s (150 ft/s)

test_procedures.acceptance_criteria: Not commonly used for metals; limited data available for some aluminum alloys and bronzes

searchable_text: Metal Test Data - Ignition and Flammability Testing Methods NASA employs three primary test methods for evaluating metallic materials' ignition and flammability in oxygen systems: promoted combustion test (upward flammability), frictional heating test, and particle impact test. The document describes test apparatus specifications, mechanical impact testing procedures, autoignition temperature methods, friction ignition testing, and particle impact testing methodologies for assessing relative material rankings and ignitability characteristics. Promoted combustion test system uses 740 cm³ stainless steel chamber pressurizable to 68.9 MPa (10,000 psia) with copper liner and aluminum promoter for ignition testing Three primary NASA test methods: promoted combustion test, frictional heating test, and particle impact test provide relative material rankings but rarely absolute ignitability information Upward flammability test (NHB 8060.1C 1991) is primary method for basic ranking of metallic materials' flammability in oxygen service Frictional heating ignitability is lower in LOX than in GOX due to low initial temperatures, but propagation is more extensive due to large oxygen quantity in condensed phase Particle impact testing uses supersonic aluminum particles at inlet pressure of 27.5 MPa (4000 psig) with target pressure varying 3.6-4.0 MPa (520-580 psia) and particle velocity 370-430 m/s Metallic powders are more likely to cause particle impact ignition than large single particles; relative material ranking assumed similar between large particles and powders Aluminum 6061  O2 304 Stainless Steel  O2 Iron  O2

title: Upward Flammability of Materials in GOX and Nonmetals Test Data
summary: This section describes the promoted combustion test for evaluating metallic material flammability in gaseous oxygen (GOX) using upward flame propagation, which provides more repeatable data than downward propagation. It also discusses nonmetals test data obtained from mechanical and pneumatic impact tests, noting that materials burn downward more readily than upward and that test conditions are typically more severe than actual use conditions.

ASTM G 63 is the guide for evaluating nonmetallic materials in oxygen service
ASTM G 72 establishes autogenous ignition temperature testing in high-pressure oxygen-enriched environments
ASTM G 86 specifies mechanical impact ignition sensitivity testing in pressurized oxygen
NASA technical memoranda (TM X-985, TM X-53533, TM X-64711) document compatibility of materials with liquid oxygen
NHB 8060.1C provides NASA requirements and test procedures for materials in combustion-supporting environments
Multiple ASTM STP volumes document flammability and sensitivity of materials in oxygen-enriched atmospheres

material_records.compatibility_notes: High ignition resistance in oxygen. Generally safe from ignition mechanisms without thin cross sections. Good for welding applications in pressure vessels and piping. Excellent for assembly housings and corrosion-resistant applications.

High ignition resistance in oxygen with improved physical properties and higher strength-to-weight ratio than Monel 400. Excellent for high hardness applications, bearing load retention, galling resistance, valve shafts, and piston shafts. Should not be welded for most applications.
Excellent material for sintered filter elements. May be used for valve bodies and components where material strength is not a prime design criterion. Good oxygen compatibility.
High strength with ignition resistance of copper-based alloys. Suitable for springs and applications requiring high strength and oxygen compatibility.
High-strength springs for elevated temperature applications. Ignition resistance and high-temperature properties vary. Use where high strength is required.
Low-strength springs for elevated temperature applications. Ignition resistance and high-temperature properties vary.
Very high-strength springs and high spring rates. Suitable for elevated temperature oxygen service.
Very high-strength springs and high spring rates for elevated temperature applications.

Very high-temperature applications where welded materials are required. High-temperature replacement for Monel 400, but with reduced material strength and increased flammability and ignition susceptibility in high-pressure oxygen environments.

Ni-Cr-Mo alloy withstanding high-temperature oxidizing environments up to 1090°C (2000°F). Resistant to mineral acids, solvents, wet and dry chlorine, and hydrofluoric acids. Markedly less flammable than C-276 in high-pressure oxygen environments. Available in cast, wrought, and forged configurations.

Ni-Cr-Mo alloy withstanding high-temperature oxidizing environments up to 1090°C (2000°F). Resistant to mineral acids, solvents, wet and dry chlorine, and hydrofluoric acids. Has flammable traits similar to Inconel 625 in high-pressure oxygen environments. More flammable than C-22 variant. Available in cast, wrought, and forged configurations.

Very common material for valves, tubing, vessels, and fittings. Provides effective and relatively low-cost material choice when ignition mechanisms are minimized or eliminated. Requires careful design to minimize ignition sources.

Very high-temperature applications with high specific strengths where welding is permitted. Can be heat-treated to enhance mechanical properties. May replace Inconel 625, but with increased flammability and ignition susceptibility in oxygen environments.

Highly susceptible to ignition and combustion in oxygen. Despite lightweight advantages, present significant ignition hazards. Anodizing surface preparation should be used for aluminum parts subject to oxygen conditions.

summary: Technical guidance on material selection for oxygen-enriched environments, covering polymers, composites, ceramics, and glasses with compatibility ratings and design considerations. All polymers are flammable in 100% oxygen and require careful ignition source management. Materials are ranked by oxygen compatibility with Teflon as most preferred for soft goods and Vespel SP-21 for bearings and seals.

key_points: All polymers are flammable in 100% oxygen requiring ignition source minimization
Teflon is most compatible soft good but lacks resilience; Viton offers shape memory advantage
Vespel SP-21 preferred for bearings, bushings, valve seats with good ignition resistance and creep resistance
Silicone and fluorosilicone not recommended due to low ignition threshold and high heat of combustion

material_records.compatibility_notes: Most compatible soft good in oxygen-enriched environments. Preferred for seals and miscellaneous components. Does not have appreciable resilience. Risk of cold flow under long-term mechanical loading and thermal cycling. Extrusion can create fine particles promoting combustion. Fillers may adversely affect ignition and combustion effects.
May replace Viton or silicone when applications call for elastomer at lower and/or higher operating temperatures than Viton.
Fluorinated material that may substitute for Teflon due to increased rigidity and slight resiliency. Vespel usually preferred over Kel-F when material strength is important.

Most recommended elastomer for oxygen usage. Has shape memory allowing it to withstand various loads and return to original shape. Reduced ignition resistance compared to Teflon but preferred for certain applications. May be preferred over Teflon for applications requiring load tolerance.
Excellent choice for bearings, bushings, valve seats, and seals. Has good ignition resistance, lubricity, machinability, and creep resistance.

Common material for seals and diaphragms at low operating temperatures (not cryogenic) and moderate pressures. Not recommended for oxygen service due to low ignition threshold in oxygen-enriched environments and high heat of combustion. All ignition sources must be eliminated if used.

Not recommended in place of standard silicone. Mechanical properties not enhanced. Ignition/flammability characteristics similar to silicone. Possible health risks from combustion byproducts increased.
Should be avoided due to high reactivity with oxygen.

Polymeric composite with enhanced mechanical properties over standard Teflon. Disadvantage is that matrix material and sizings are more flammable in oxygen. Complete ignition sensitivity testing must be performed before use.

Not generally flammable in oxygen, serve as effective thermal and electrical insulators. May be severely degraded by contact with molten metal slag compromising fire stop or insulation ability. Typically brittle and susceptible to fracture from manufacturing defects and impact loading. High safety factors and compressive loading required.

May be used for pressure vessel windows and valve seals. Pressure vessel codes require glass-retaining pressure differentials to have safety factors of ten or greater. Special design features must be incorporated per ASME. Suitable for many applications.
Often used for windows as well as for valve ball seals where they mate against seats. Preferred option for high-performance applications.

title: Design Practices to Prevent Ignition in Oxygen Systems
summary: This section provides comprehensive design guidance for preventing ignition hazards in GOX (gaseous oxygen) systems by addressing mechanical impact, frictional heating, electrical arcing, particulate generation, and component design considerations. Key strategies include eliminating burrs and sharp edges, avoiding rotating valve stems, eliminating blind passages, and preventing seal rotation to minimize fuel sources and ignition opportunities in oxygen-enriched environments.

As

which

rate
and

heating
of the
seals.
Mechanical
Impact.
Any
situation
where
mechanical
components
can
impact
against
each
other
should
be
avoided.
Examples
of
situations
where
this
can
occur
are
relief
valves,
shut-off
valves,
and
regulators.
Spring-loaded
seats
in these
devices
react
against
fluid
pressures,
and,
during
transient
flow
situations,
the
seal
and
seat
can
impact
against
each
other
caused
by
the
imposed
force

Refer
to Figure

which

a place
where
mechanical
impact
could
occur.
Frictional
Heatine.
Rotational
or translational
sliding
contact
between
two
parts
has the
potential
to generate
enough
heat
to ignite
parts
at the
interface.
Common
configurations
where
this
situation
can
occur
is with
bearings
and
pistons.
Any
contamination,
such
as lubrication
or
particulate
generated
by
seal
wear,
near
the heated
region
can
also
be ignited.
Frictional
heating
hazards
can be
reduced
by
careful
control
of surface
finishes,
coefficients
of
friction,
alignment,
and
flow-induced
cooling.
Rubbing
of metallic
parts
should
be
avoided
unless
the
design
has been
carefully
analyzed.
Frictional
heating
has also
been
found
to ignite
materials
in cryogenic
applications.
The
frictional
heat
can
vaporize
the LOX
and
form
a vapor-rich
fluid
surrounding
the
heat
source.
Once
this
occurs,
the ignition
and
combustion
situation
resembles
that
of
a GOX
situation.
The
force
imbalances
across
the valve
seat
configuration
shown
in Figure

could
create
friction
when
closing
the valve

Electrical
Arcing.
Electrical
arcs
in oxygen-enriched
environments
can
lead
to heating
and
subsequent
ignition.
An example
of
good
design
practice
is found
in Figure

which
demonstrates
the proper
method
to insulate
electrical
components
and
reduce

of arcing.
Arcing
can
rapidly

wire

creating

and
heating
in the presence

causing

Eliminate
Burrs
and
Sharp_ Edges.
Although
the
elimination
of burrs
and
sharp
edges
should
be
the
goal
of all
designers
and
machine
shops,
this
becomes
especially
important
in oxygen
systems
where
small,
thin
portions
of
metal
can
become
the
site for
kindling
chain
combustion.
If an ignition
source
such
as particle
impact
is able
to
ignite
a burr,
this
may
promote
the
combustion
of the bulkier
material

gl

surrounding

would
otherwise
have
been
substantially
more
difficult
to

(Figure

Use-Generated

Threaded
connections
can
generate
contaminants
in oxygen
systems
as they
are
engaged
and
tightened
(Figure
C-6a).
This
problem
can
be
eliminated
by
redesigning
the
threaded
members
so the
smooth
portion
of the
plug
interfaces
with
the
seal
before
the
threads
engage
(Figure
C-6b).
However,
this
solution
involves
rotating
a part
against
its
seal
and
may
cause
seal
damage.
Alternatively,
the
in-line
threaded
connection
can
be replaced
with
a flanged
and
bolted
connection
in which
the
threaded
portions
are
outside
the
fluid
stream
(Figure
C-6c).
The
function
of the
threaded
connection
can
also
be
performed
by a separate
locking
nut
and
sealing
plug;
the
locking
nut
is
inserted
after
the
sealing
plug
has
been
pushed
into
the
seal
(Figure
C-6d).
A
fifth
option
is to install
a barrier
ring
to block
the particulate
(Figure

Avoid
Rotating
Valve
Stem_.
A manual,
screw-type
valve
with
a rotating
stem
(Figure
C-7a)
might
seem
desirable
in a high-pressure
oxygen
system
because
such
a valve
can
provide
a
slow
actuation
rate.
However,
a rotating-stem
valve
presents
contamination
problems.
A nonmetallic
seat
can
easily
be damaged
by
excessive
closing
torque,
shredding,
or gas
erosion
during
opening
and
closing.
Furthermore,
solid
contaminants
can
become
embedded
in soft
seat
material.
If the
seat
is
made
of metal,
it must
be hardened
to prevent
galling
when
the
valve
stem
rotates
against
the seat.
Such
hardened
materials
can
fracture
or
even
fragment
as
a result
of excessive
dosing
torque
or
closure
onto
hard
contaminants
such
as silica.
A manual
valve
with
a nonrotating
stem
(Figure
C-7b)
and
a metallic
seat
can
be
used
to achieve
the desired
slow
actuation
rate.
In this
case,
the
metal
seat
can
be
made
of a much
softer
material
and
the
seat
can
be formed
by
"coining"
(pressure
molding
by
the stem
itself
to create
a perfect
match).
Contaminants
will
not
cause
fragmentation
of
such
a seat.
Galling
cannot
occur
unless
the
nonrotating
feature
is compromised
(therefore,
care
should
be
exercised
when
cleaning).
The
seat
and
body
of
such
a valve
can
be
fabricated
from
many
metals
that
are comparatively
unreactive
with
oxygen.
Eliminate
Blind
Passages
and
Crevices.
A stagnant
area
at the end of
a drilled
passage
tends
to collect
debris
either
from
manufacture
or from
normal
use.
During
rapid
pressurization
of
GOX
and
its attendant
compression
heating,
the
debris
becomes
fuel
for
ignition.
When
an underexpanded
jet
impinges
on (or
flows
across)
a stagnant
cavity,
a
periodic
pressure
wave
may
be
formed
that
oscillates
in the
cavity,
heating
the
C-7

--- Page 210 ---
j.
gas
within
it (cavity
resonance).
If particles
are present
in regions
of
rapid gas
flow,
they
can
impact
the end of the passage
and
cause
ignition
of
the
component,
drill
points
can
collect
particulate
at their
center
and
significantly
increase
the
chance
of
ignition.
Blind
passages
and
dead-end
cavities
also
increase
cleaning
difficulty,
requiring
that
the part be turned
during
soaking
to
eliminate
air pockets.
Special
nozzles
or extensions
must
be used
to flush
such
areas.
Figure
C-Sa
depicts
a blind
passage
created
by plugging
a drilled
passage.
Figure
C-8b
depicts
a dead-end
cavity
created
by overdrilling
an
intersecting
passage.
GOX
components
should
be designed
so that
a jet will
not
impinge
on or flow
across
a stagnant
cavity.
Jets should
be gradually
expanded
and
stagnant
cavities
should
be
eliminated
or kept as
shallow
as possible.
In Figure
C-Sa,
the
blind
passage
could
be
eliminated
by
making
the
counterbore
for
the plug
much
deeper
and
installing
the plug
closer
to the
regulator
stem.
The
cavity
may
not be
completely
eliminated,
but the total
dead
volume
would
be
significantly
reduced.
The
cavity
shown
in Figure
C-Sb
can
be eliminated
by
paying
careful
attention
to dimensions
and
tolerances
or,
preferably,
by
redesigning
to eliminate
the
intersecting
holes.
If particle
impact
ignition
is a
concern,
the
drill
point
should
be
eliminated
as part of the
redesign.
Inspection
with
a borescope
can
be conducted
to verify
that
passageway
lengths
are
within
tolerance.
Prevent
Rotation
of Seals
and
Rotation
Against
Scats.
Sealed
parts
that
require
rotation
at assembly (such
as O-rings
on threaded
shafts)
can
generate
particles
which
may
migrate
into
the flow
stream
(Figure
C-9a).
Particulate
generation
also
occurs
in ball
valves
where
a ball
is
rotated
on a nonmetallic
seat.
A related
phenomenon,
which
may
be
described
as
"feathering,"
occurs
when
valve
stems
are
rotated
against
some
nonmetallic
seats
such
as
Kel-l_.
Because
of
the
mechanical
properties
of
some
nonmetallic
materials,
a thin,
feather-like
projection
of
material
is extruded
from
the
seat.
The
feathered
feature
is more
ignitable
than
the
seat
itself.
Instead
of rotating,
the
sealed
part
can
be designed
as
a push-in
plug
locked
in
place
by a second
part
that
is threaded
but
not
sealed,
as
shown
in
Figure
C-9b.
Alternately,
the
sealed
threads
can
be replaced
with
a flanged
and
bolted
connection.
Kel-F*
and
other
nonmetallic
materials
subject
to
feathering
should
not
be
used
for
seals
and
seats
in rotating
configurations.
Ball
valves
are
not
recommended
for
oxygen
systems
because
of
their
tendency
to generate
particulate
and
their
quick
opening
times.
The
quick
opening
times
lead
to rapid
pressurization
of downstream
cavities,
creating
rapid
heating
of
soft
goods
and
increasing
the risk
of polymer
ignition
and
combustion.

key_points: Mechanical impact in relief valves, shut-off valves, and regulators should be avoided through careful force balance analysis
Frictional heating from rotating or translating sliding contact can ignite materials and is particularly hazardous in cryogenic LOX applications where vaporization creates GOX-like conditions
Electrical arcing in oxygen-enriched environments requires insulation of electrical components to prevent ignition of wire insulation
Burrs and sharp edges serve as kindling sites for chain combustion and should be eliminated in all oxygen system designs
Threaded connections generate particulate contamination; alternatives include flanged and bolted connections or barrier rings
Rotating valve stems cause nonmetallic seat damage and particulate generation; nonrotating stems with metallic seats are preferred
Blind passages and dead-end cavities collect debris and are subject to cavity resonance heating; design should eliminate or minimize such features
Seal rotation during assembly and ball valve operation generate ignitable particulates; push-in plug designs and flanged connections are alternatives
Materials subject to feathering (e.g., Kel-F) should not be used in rotating seal configurations
Ball valves are not recommended for oxygen systems due to particulate generation and rapid pressurization effects

title: Design Considerations for Oxygen System Safety - Thin Walls, Sharp Edges, and Seal Extrusion
summary: This section addresses critical design hazards in oxygen systems including thin-walled structures that can rupture under pressure and expose reactive bare metal, sharp edges at hole intersections that concentrate particle impact heating, and seal extrusion issues. The document emphasizes risk optimization through careful dimensional tolerance studies, CAD modeling, stress analysis, and strategic material selection to minimize ignition hazards in high-pressure oxygen environments.

Particle impact at sharp edges and orifice intersections can generate near-sonic velocity impacts that efficiently convert kinetic energy to heat and initiate combustion
Drill point intersections exaggerate heating by concentrating energy from multiple burning particles and promoting kindling chain combustion

Risk optimization may require incorporating higher-quality materials, adding filters, and reducing pressurization rates despite design constraints

test_procedures.test_purpose: Verify system integrity and functional capabilities before oxygen service operation
test_procedures.acceptance_criteria: Test pressure must not exceed system MAWP; components must pass flow and functional capability verification; components previously not qualified for oxygen service must be disassembled and inspected

test_procedures.test_purpose: Establish system pressure integrity and verify container and attachment compliance with applicable codes
test_procedures.acceptance_criteria: Must meet requirements of NHB 1700.6 (1976); hydrostatic testing recommended as safer and more reliable than pneumatic testing; must be completed before cleaning per Chapter 5

test_procedures.test_name: Boiloff Rate and Heat Leak Measurement
test_procedures.test_purpose: Establish maximum allowable hauling distance of liquid-oxygen transportation system by measuring boiloff rate and system heat leak
test_procedures.acceptance_criteria: Boiloff tests must be repeated after minimum 1600 km (1000 miles) trailer operation; one-way travel time calculation per 49 CFR (1986)

test_procedures.test_purpose: Detect leaks in LOX/GOX systems using soap film method
test_procedures.acceptance_criteria: Sensitivity of approximately 10^-3 cm³/s (6 x 10^-5 in³/sec); systems must be checked initially at atmospheric temperature and when loaded under MAWP

test_procedures.test_purpose: Detect leaks in inner vessel and system assemblies with highest sensitivity available for industrial applications
test_procedures.acceptance_criteria: Must be performed before oxygen system filling; sensitivity set at 1 x 10^-9 std cm³/s (6 x 10^-11 in³/s); no-leak indication for 15 minutes constitutes successful test

test_procedures.test_purpose: Verify vacuum integrity and insulation stability of vacuum-jacketed equipment
test_procedures.acceptance_criteria: Vacuum space pumped to minimum 30-mm Hg and sealed; pressure rise must not exceed 5-mm Hg during 48-hour holding period; higher rise indicates potential leak or outgassing of H2O saturated perlite in annulus

test_procedures.test_name: Flight-Weight (Class III) Pressure Vessel Qualification and Acceptance

test_procedures.test_purpose: Verify system and component cleanliness at operating levels
test_procedures.acceptance_criteria: Initial testing may be performed with clean inert fluids; acceptance tests may be done with nitrogen; life tests must be conducted with oxygen

Flexible hoses require hydrostatic testing before initial use and visual recertification at least every 5 years with permanent imprinting of test pressure and expiration date

Compliance with regulations and standards required for personnel and facility safety Federal regulations originate from Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) through DOT, OSHA, and U.S. Coast Guard 49 CFR (1986) designates DOT rule-making and enforcement bodies for interstate shipping of LOX and compressed gases Regulations are mandatory; standards and guidelines are published by industrial and governmental organizations DOT, FAA, Coast Guard, and Office of Hazardous Materials have adopted published guidelines for LOX handling

title: Section E.6-E.8: Codes, Standards, and Regulatory Organizations for Oxygen Safety
summary: This section outlines the organizational framework for oxygen safety standards and practices, including rules developed by NASA and national laboratories, codes and standards from nonprofit associations and professional societies, and a comprehensive listing of responsible groups and their applicable regulatory documents. Key organizations include ANSI, API, ASME, CGA, NFPA, and various federal government agencies that establish mandatory and advisory provisions for oxygen system design, construction, and operation.

title: Appendix F: Scaling Laws, Explosions, Blasts, and Fragments
summary: This section provides a comprehensive review of accidental explosions and scaling laws, characterizing explosions by type and discussing blast wave behavior. It introduces point-source blast wave theory with three regions of interest (near-field, intermediate, and far-field) and presents Sach's cube-root scaling law for predicting blast wave properties at various distances from an explosion.

searchable_text: Blast Wave Properties and Fragmentation Analysis for Oxygen and Hydrogen Explosions This section discusses blast wave characteristics from accidental LOX-liquid hydrogen explosions, including TNT equivalence ratios at various pressure levels and fragmentation patterns from bursting oxygen pressure vessels. The analysis provides dimensionless parameters for predicting blast properties and references methods for estimating fragment velocity distributions and ranges. TNT equivalence for LOX-liquid hydrogen explosions varies by pressure level: 0.07 at >103.4 kPa, 1.0 at 101.4-0.69 kPa, and 2.0 at <0.69 kPa At 101.4 kPa and above, approximately 6.5 kg of LOX-liquid hydrogen produces equivalent pressure-distance effects as 0.45 kg of TNT Fragment characteristics from bursting oxygen vessels depend on total energy released, release rate, and pressure vessel design Liquid-propellant explosions differ significantly from TNT explosions, making TNT equivalence approximations inexact Ground systems generate fewer fragments than flight systems due to differences in pressure vessel materials and construction

APPENDIX
H
GLOSSARY
ACCEPTANCE
TEST.
A standard
test that leads
to certification
of a component
or system.
ADIABATIC.
A process
by which
the
system
changes
state
without
thermal
energy
exchange
between
the
system
and
the surroundings.
ADIABATIC
COMPRESSION.
Mechanical
work
transferred
to a system,
where
the
energy
goes
into
increasing
the internal
energy
of the
material
for a static
system
or increasing
the
enthalpy
for
a dynamic
system.
If the process
is also
reversible
(in the thermodynamic
definition),
this
change
is also
isentropic.
AUTOIGNITION.
The
phenomenon
in which
a mixture
of
gases,
vapors,
mists,
dusts,
or
sprays
ignites
spontaneously
with
no external
ignition
source.
It is frequently
called
"autogenous
ignition"
or
"spontaneous
ignition."
AUTOIGNITION
TEMPERATURE
(AIT).
The
lowest
temperature
at which
material
will
spontaneously
ignite
(autogenous
ignition).
BLAST
WAVE.
A shock
wave
in air,
which
has
degenerated
as the
shock
front
becomes
less
dense.
BLAST
YIELD.
Energy
released
in an explosion,
inferred
from
measurements
of the
characteristics
of the blast
waves
generated
by
the
explosion.
BUDDY
SYSTEM.
A system
used
in hazardous
operations
where
one
person
performs
the
necessary
task
while
another
person
standing
nearby
is fully
prepared
(clothing,
training,
etc.)

the primary
person
from

area
in case
of incapacitation.
BURN
VELOCITY.
The
velocity
of propagation
of a flame
through
a flammable
material.
Bum
velocities
are
absolute
velocities
measured
relative
to the velocity
of
the
unburned
material;
flame
speeds
are
measured
in laboratory
coordinates
and
are
not
absolute.
BURST
PRESSURE.
The
pressure
at which
a gas
storage
vessel
or burst
disk
bursts
or
fails.
CARGO
TANK.
Any
container
designed
to be permanently
attached
to any
motor
vehicle
or
other
highway
vehicle
and
in which
any
compressed
gas
is to be
transported.
The
term
"cargo
tank"
does
not
include
any
tank used
solely
to supply
fuel
for
the
vehicle
or
containers
fabricated
for
cylinders.
CATASTROPHIC
FAILURE.
One
that
causes
complete
and
irreparable
loss
of
function
of
a component
or system.
Structural
failure
of
a pressure
vessel
is a catastrophic
failure.

The
documentation
that qualifies
a vessel
or
system
to operate
in the
intended
service.
CLEANLINESS
LEVEL.
An established
maximum
of allowable
contaminants
based
on
sized
distribution,
or quantity
on a given

Also,
an

of

and nonparticulate
matter
visible
under
visible
light
and/or
UV
illumination.
COLD
INJURY.
An
injury
caused
by
freezing
of skin
tissue
caused
by exposure
to a very
cold
atmosphere,
surface,
or cryogenic.
Also
referred
to as a "cryogenic
bum."
COMBUSTIBLE
LIQUID.
A liquid
with
a flash
point
at or above
333
K (140
OF).
COMBUSTIBLE
SOLID.
A solid
that can burn
in the
presence
of an oxidizer.
CONFINED
SPACES.
A confined
space
is not
normally
occupied
by personnel.
It has
limited
or restricted
openings
for

and
exit,
may
lack
adequate
ventilation,
and

contain
or produce
"dangerous
air contamination;"

CONTAMINANT.
A foreign
substance
that
can
have

effects
on
system
operation,

or reliability.
CRITICAL
SURFACE.
A surface
that requires
precision
cleaning.
CRYOGEN.
Substances
which
boil
at extremely
low
temperatures,
usually
at or below
-150
°C.
CRYOGENIC
PROPELLANTS.
Propellants
that
are
gases
at ambient
temperature
and
pressure,
but have
been
liquified
by chilling
to or below
-150
°C
and
pressurization.
EARTH-STORABLE
PROPELLANTS.
Propellants
that
are
in the

or solid
state at
ambient
temperature
and
pressure.

axe or spark

and

equilibration

pressure

fluids

rapid

reaetions

large
volumes
of hot
gases.

compound

mechanical
mixture

when

undergoes
a very
rapid
combustion
or decomposition

large
volumes
of heated
gases
that
exert
pressure
on the
surrounding
medium.

--- Page 271 ---
EXPLOSIVE YIELD.
Energy
released
in an
explosion.
It is often
expressed
as a percent
or
fraction
of the
energy
that
would
be released
by the
same
mass
of
a standard
high
explosive
such
as TNT.
FAILURE
MODE
AND
EFFECTS
ANALYSIS
(FMEA).
A systematic,
methodical
analysis
performed
to identify
and
document
all identifiable
failure
modes
at a prescribed
level
and
to
specify
the
resultant
effect
of the
modes
of failure.
FIRE
RESISTANT.
Materials
that
will
resist
burning
when
contacted
by
fuels
or oxidizers,
but
will
eventually
burn
after
continuous
contact
and
exposure
to an ignition
source.
FLAMMABLE
LIQUID.
Any
liquid
with
a flash
point
below
300
K (80
°F)
as determined
by
standard
methods
(ASTM
D 56
1985;
ASTM
D 92
1985).
FLASH
POINT.
The
lowest
temperature,
corrected
to
I01.3
kPa
(I.00
atm),
at which
an
ignition
source
under
specified
conditions,
causes
the
material
vapor
to ignite
momentarily.
FAILURE
RATE.
The
number
of
failures
of an
item
per
unit
measure
of
use
(cycles,
time,
miles,
events,
etc.,
as
applicable
for
the item).
FLOW
CAPACITY.
The
flow
capacity
of a pressure-relief
device
is determined
at the
flow
rating
pressure,
expressed
in cubic
feet
per
minute
of free
air
discharge.
FRAGMENTATION.
The
breaking
up of
the confining
material
when
an explosion
takes
place.
Fragments
may
be complete
items,
subassemblies,
pieces
of material,
or pieces
of
equipment
or buildings
containing
the flame.
GEYSERING.
Geysering
occurs
in vertical
systems
with
a tank
and
a long
feedline
from
the
tank
filled
with
cryogenic
oxygen.
Heat
transfer
into
the line
causes
gas
bubbles
to form
and
begin
rising
in the line.
As the bubbles
rise,
they
coalesce
to form
larger
bubbles.
In a line
long
with
respect
to its diameter,
the result
is an expanding
vapor
bubble
of
sufficient
size
to
expel
the
liquid
above
it into
the tank
with
a force
large
enough
at times
to rupture
the
tank
or to damage
internal

1.0 
PURPOSE 
 
This John C. Stennis Space Center (SSC) standard (SSTD) establishes compatibility 
requirements for materials used in liquid oxygen (LOX) and gaseous oxygen (GOX) service in 
facilities at SSC. 
 
2.0 
APPLICABILITY  
 
This SSTD applies to  all National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) personnel, 
contractors, and subcontractors dealing with materials used in LOX/GOX service at SSC. 
 
3.0 
REFERENCES AND APPLICABLE DOCUMENTS 
 
All references are assumed to be the latest version unless otherwise indicated.

and Maintenance

and the applicable documents referenced therein.

5.0 
REQUIREMENTS 
 
5.1 
Safety 
 
NASA/SSC and its contractors shall abide by Oxygen Standard (ASTM Manual 36) for 
all safety issues regarding LOX and GOX systems. 
 
5.2 
LOX And GOX Systems 
 
a. All SSC LOX and GOX Fluid Distribution Systems shall be designed and maintained 
in accordance with the materials selection criteria in NASA STD 6001. 
 
b. The Materials Selection List (MSL) of SSC Control Drawing 54000-GM30 identifies 
non-metallic materials that are exempt from the NASA STD 6001 impact (batch) test 
requirements and specifies the use parameters under which the exemption applies for 
each of the listed materials. 
 
c. The guidance provided by KTI-5210 shall be used in selecting and evaluating 
metallic materials for oxygen service. 
 
d. Throttling valve applications at pressures above 6000 psig require a plug made of 
Monel 400, Monel K500, or equivalent material having high resistance to ignition and 
combustion (flame propagation) in high pressure enriched oxygen environments. A 
Material Usage Agreement (MUA) is required for valve applications not meeting this 
requirement.   
 
5.3 
Material Usage Agreement (MUA) 
 
a. Each MUA shall be prepared and processed for reviews, revisions as needed, and 
approval in accordance with SOI-8080-0016. 
 
b. If a non-metallic material is not included on the MSL or its use parameter exceeds 
that covered by the MSL, the material shall be used only with the authority of an 
approved MUA, Form SSC-716. For purposes of this SSTD, a composite material, 
where at least one of its constituent materials is a non-metal, is also classified as a 
non-metallic material. 
 
c. For all cases where a metallic material is not listed as a recommended material for 
oxygen service or if it is to be used at a service pressure that exceeds the listed 
“PROMOTED IGNITION HIGHEST NO BURN PRESSURE” in KTI-5210, the 
material shall be evaluated and controls shall be implemented to minimize the

d. For materials fitting the description of Section 5.3b, an approved MUA is required for 
use in oxygen service if any of the following applies: 
 
1. Prior history of successful use of the material in oxygen service does not exist; 
2. Certified and accredited oxygen compatibility test data for the material type is not 
available; or 
3. Material is to be used in an application, environment, or configuration that is 
more prone to ignition than those of previous historical and operational oxygen 
systems and components where the respective material was used. 
 
NOTE: 
Type 304, 304L, 304/304L, 316, 316L, 316/316L, 321, 347, 17-4PH, 
Nitronic 40 and Nitronic 60 stainless steels and selected aluminum-bronze 
alloys have been used successfully at NASA/SSC in liquid (cold 
supercritical) oxygen services at pressures up to 8500 psig and in gaseous 
oxygen services at pressures up to 3000 psig. Because these materials can 
ignite and burn in oxygen environments at pressures well below 3000 psig, 
it was necessary to implement design configuration and material 
processing controls, including the processing of MUAs for selected 
materials and applications, to assure successful and safe use of these 
materials. 
 
6.0 
RECORDS AND FORMS 
 
Records and forms required by the procedures of this standard shall be maintained in accordance 
with SPR 1440.1.  All records and forms are assumed to be the latest edition unless otherwise 
indicated.  Forms may be obtained from the SSC Electronic Forms repository or from the NASA 
SSC Forms Management Officer.  Quality Records are identified in the SSC Master Records
